speechtext: I desire to acquaint the government with the fact that hon. members are getting telegrams from the civil servants all over the country, who are very disappointed at not getting the flat increase of SI 20. I should lake to know if the government are going to make a statement on the matter before parliament prorogues?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
It is quite true, as the hon. gentleman has said, that he has been receiving telegrams on this subject; we all have. Now, the government have gone carefully and sympathetically into the question of increasing the salaries of the civil servants. If the civil service of Canada is not satisfied it seems to me it is about time for some person to say a word on behalf of the tax-payers, and to inform the hon. gentleman and others that if the civil servants are not satisfied with the increases as granted, it will be very easy for the government to withdraw the measure. I am told that yesterday in the Senate a measure of interest to the civil service, a measure to extend once more the time for them to come in under the Superannuation Act, was under consideration, and that certain changes were made at the instance of the organized civil service which may delay the measure. This morning I asked the departmental officials to prepare for me an estimate as to what the changes will cost, 
and I say now to hon. gentlemen that unless I have full details so as to advise the government with respect to the additional cost, I will not proceed with that measure this year.

CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENT Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved the second reading of Bill No. 304, to amend the Canada Shipping Act.

I
wish to speak against not what the bill contains but what it does not contain. I do not -think there is in the whole range of our statutes any -act which so decidedly requires changing and remodelling as this one. It goes back to the days when internal combustion engines were unknown. It is obsolete in every sense of the word. It has been due for repeal and reenactment any time during the last- twenty years and yet nothing has been done. As'far back as 1908 the need was so apparent and urgent that a comprehensive and, I think, in many respects a suitable bill was drafted. Perhaps on account of the war or other causes the matter was postponed; but that is nearly twenty years ago, and we are still waiting for the reenactment of reasonable legislation in regard to these very important matters.
From one end of Canada to the other the shipping interests, seamen, masters, mates and so on are vitally concerned in the changes required in this 'bill. I think in 1924 or 1925, certainly in 1925, there is recorded on Hansard a definite promise that a bill would be formulated in the recess; that it would be submitted to the shipping interests concerned for their advice and opinion, and that it would be brought forward at the next session. That was in 1925; this is 1927 and what have we here to-day? A trumpery little amendment concerning the prohibition of touts on boats or wharves connected with the ships, while interests of infinite importance require attention.
I do not blame the minister at the head of this department because this concerns matters with which he cannot be very familiar. There is in his department a great deal of deadwood which is much in need of revivifying. The settled policy, in every instance when progress or reform is suggested, appears to be, to do nothing. Last year we heard a great deal about the customs scandal; but there is such a thing as scandal which originates not in wrongdoing, but in inaction, standing still, stagnation. This matter should be attended to at an early date. It is too late now. I presume, to do anything this session,
but I take this opportunity of urging on the government that the advancement of British Columbia, which is so largely dependent upon the operation of matters connected with the seacoast, is being held back for lack of attention, not only in this 'but in several other matters as well.

I wish to protest against the principle of this bill. It may be all right as regards ocean navigation, but I see no necessity for this legislation in connection with ships on the inland lakes and rivers. This is simply going to create a monopoly on ships and on shore as well. I doubt very much the right of this parliament to enact legislation of this kind as affecting navigation on the great lakes. At Niagara ports where a million people a year travel backwards and forwards, they have public docks where anybody can go and solicit business. This is going to give a monopoly of the tourist business to the big corporations that control not only the vessels but hotels and every other agency in places where there is a huge United States tourist traffic. I do know that such lake ports as Buffalo, Cleveland and Detroit, have no regulations similar to this. As this legislation is going to create a monopoly I wish to protest against it.

I have been given to understand that under the Canada Shipping Act there is a possibility that navigation proceeding from Ontario ports will be compelled to pay pilotage dues. This is the only part of the country in proximity to the St. Lawrence river which is compelled to do so. I understand a boat from Newfoundland or any other port can come here through the St. Lawrence without paying pilotage dues and that only boats from Ontario, whether they use pilots or not, have to pay pilotage dues. Before this bill is passed I should like to know from the minister if that is authorized by the Canada Shipping Act. In other words, is a straight discrimination against Ontario contained in the Canada Shipping Act?

There may be something
in the observations of the hon. member for Kingston City, but it can hardly come under this bill. My hon. friend will have an opportunity of discussing the matter when we take up the departmental estimates which will be considered immediately after this. There is an item for pilotage on which the discussion can very well take place. The complaint of the hon. gentleman is not new; a similar complaint has already been made because Ontario boats navigating from the great lakes
Canada Shipping Act

down to Montreal have been forced to pay pilotage dues. That is in accordance with the act. We have what we call pilotage dues, and every vessel going down from Montreal to Quebec has to take a pilot on board or at least to pay the amount required by the act for pilots' fees. According to the law, there is compulsory payment of pilotage dues not only in Quebec but in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. It is a fact that vessels from the great lakes going down to Quebec or below have to pay pilotage dues.
Mr. Speaker-
The hon. gentleman has already spoken. He can speak in committee on the bill.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went (into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Soliciting for hotels, lodging houses, etc., on ships or wharves, without written consent.

I wish to protest against the action of the government in bringing down such an unimportant and unnecessary amendment as this when the consideration of other far more important amendments to the Canada Shipping Act has been refused. I think this bill should be sent back to the department, that such unfair discrimination should be discouraged, and that other far more necessary amendments to the act should be brought in. It is quite clear that the act needs repair work of some kind, but this little bit of an amendment, in the absence of other far more important amendments, should not be allowed to go through. I understand that the international section of the St. Lawrence is under a different system, and that if a boat comes down, she can take on a pilot or not just as she sees fit, and she is not charged for the pilot. I consider this legislation before us is very unfair, because it discriminates against navigation on the Ontario lakes.

So far as the clause we are now studying is concerned, I think it is a desirable piece of legislation. Whether my hon. friend is correct in saying that it should come under provincial legislation, I am not competent to say, but the matter dealt with here is important. However, I agree with what the hon. member for Kingston and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni have said in regard to the necessity for amendments to the Canada Shipping Act. The act is certainly in need of a complete renovation; it ought to be revised throughout, and I would

urge upon the government that during the coming recess a very careful study should be made of the act, and a bill be prepared and brought down early next session, because it will be a very, very extensive bill, and will take months of committee work to get it in proper shape, so it ought to be introduced at the earliest possible date in the session, and referred to a special committee. I do not know of many other statutes of equal importance; perhaps the Railway Act would be a parallel case. But as far as this particular measure is concerned, I have no objection to it; in fact, I must say that for some years I have recognized that this legislation is required. It is pretty late in the session to discuss whether this is constitutional or not. The provision here, I think, is a necessary one, and I would urge upon the minister to take into consideration what a number of members have said, and what I have just said, in regard to the necessity for a general revision of the act.

I agree that there is a necessity for the passage of this bill. The practice of touting on these boats has become in the nature of a public nuisance, and it is to remedy that nuisance that this bill is introduced.
In regard to the Canada Shipping Act, which we seek to amend by this bill, I endorse what has been said by other hon. members. The act is certainly due for revision. I have heard it discussed by men who are more familiar with it than I am, and I have heard it condemned because many of its sections are said to be obsolete; many, it is charged, are beyond the jurisdiction of this parliament, others are contradictory, and there are a great many omissions which should be supplied in the act. But the question at once arises, is this the proper time for a revision? The larger question of the Merchant Shipping Act, an imperial act, has been referred to a special committee of experts, under the recommendations of the recent Imperial conference, and I doubt very much whether we could usefully revise the Canada Shipping Act until we have the results of the investigation of that committee of experts before us. Undoubtedly there are many omissions which could be supplied now, but I think the general revision of the whole act should stand until we know just where we are at in regard to our jurisdiction in the matter.
Mr- TOLMIE:	I quite agree with what
has been said concerning the necessity for a revision of the Canada Shipping Act. An act of that kind should be revised from time to time, in view of the changing conditions

Canada Shipping Act
and the rapid development of our commerce, particularly on the Pacific coast, but I think before a complete revision of the act is undertaken we should have before us, as my leader has pointed out, the results of the work of the special committee appointed under the Imperial conference to amend the Merchant Shipping Act.
With regard to this particular amendment, I want to endorse it. We are doing a tremendous tourist trade on the Pacific coast. We have excellent ships belonging to the Princess line, for instance, operated by the Canadian Pacific, and many other very good boats engaged in tourist traffic from the American boundary right up to Alaska, and calling at our Canadian ports. These ships bring tens of thousands of people during the tourist season, and it is a great nuisance to these tourists, travelling as many of them are for a rest, to be canvassed and bothered by solicitors of various kinds. In addition to that, the companies that operate these boats try to keep them nice and tidy and clean, but if solicitors are to be permitted to canvass on them, the boats will be littered up with advertising material of all kinds, and it will be impossible to keep them, in decent shape. I think that anyone wishing to solicit either on the boats or on the wharves of the shipping companies should first obtain the permission that is made necessary in this bill.

I contend, Mr. Speaker, that it is outside the jurisdiction of this parliament to pass this legislation except as to navigation on the gulf and ocean ports. To apply it to Ontario is a ridiculous proposition. In the Niagara district, the Muskoka district and the Brockville district, the services rendered by some of these tourist transportation organizations is of the utmost-convenience to the travelling public. Dear knows we are trying hard enough to get more American tourists, and this legislation, if applied to tourist traffic on the Ontario lakes, will greatly inconvenience the travelling public.
I would like to know who has asked for this legislation. We are charged on this side of the House with being the party of the big interests. I would ask what big interests are behind this bill? The Canada Steamship Company came to the police commissioners in the city of Toronto some time ago and asked us to pass just such a regulation as this. We did not need it in Toronto because we have an association of all the hotels and tourist bodies, working together
in harmony for the good of the travelling public, and that is a great convenience to the travelling public. I doubt very much whether this parliament has power to pass this legislation, as it is in restraint of trade. What does the Justice department say about this bill? If .they were consulted, I believe they would say that this parliament has no power to pass legislation affecting inland waters. The city of Toronto has spent millions of dollars to take over wharves, and the Toronto Terminals Company are running bus services where they cannot get a service from the National Railways, and are they to be prevented from going on the wharves which they have paid for themselves, just because the Canada Steamships Company wants this thing? Is the minister going to drive all the tourist business into the hands of the big corporations? The Canadian National Railways are doing this very same thing on their trains and boats. There is no demand for this legislation, and it would only lead to litigation, and furthermore it will do away with what is now a real convenience to the travelling public. It may be necessary .to have some regulation of this kind with regard to ocean traffic, but it is an absurdity to apply it to the tourist trade on the inland lakes, and I say that this amendment should stand over till next session.

There is no doubt in the mind of the legal officer of the department that we have absolute jurisdiction to pass an amendment of this character. As long as Canada has full jurisdiction in regard to all navigation on inland waters as well as on the ocean, we have the power and the authority to say who shall be prevented from going on any of the ships under the control of the Canada Shipping Act.
I quite agree with hon. members who have spoken in regard to amending the act. The act is due for revision. The matter has been considered for a few years in the department, but we have had such rapid development in the last few years that it has been found that a provision that was adequate two or three years ago will not meet the present situation. New devices have been introduced in navigation.
The hon. leader of the opposition is quite right when he states that it would be useless to proceed to deal with the Canada Shipping Act when there is a commission dealing with the same matter. After the commission makes its report we will be in a better position to deal with the question, and we all agree that it is necessary to amend this very important
Canada Shipping Act

act. The proposed amendment now before the committee is of a non-contentious nature; it has been asked for by the transportation companies and it is not intended to embarrass the tourist traffic. On the contrary it will help the tourist traffic, because it will prevent certain people going on the boats and worrying the passengers in regard to hotels and lodging houses. We want the passengers on the boats to be free. If any man is allowed to go on the boat to advertise hotels he should have the consent of the proprietor of the ship on which he wishes to advertise.

I think there is a good deal in what the minister says, that passengers should not be annoyed by agents of any kind, but I think there is one feature of the situation which he has not considered. For instance, in my district one navigation concern is privately owned and another is a company, both in the tourist business. Does the minister not see that there is a possibility of the company in the navigation business and the company in the tourist business working hand in hand in dealing with the tourist traffic. They would have the power to send the traffic wherever they pleased, although they might not do it. They would be shutting out competition and working an injury in that way. Would the minister consider that aspect of the case?

I do not see any serious danger in that, because I have enough confidence in those operating the boats to feel that they will not prevent legitimate advertisement. The only thing these people have to do is to go to the office of the company and ask for a permit. If a reputable citizen goes to a company asking permission to distribute literature on the boat, I cannot imagine that the company would refuse him permission.
If the minister will assure me that they would get that right-
I am sure they would get it
It is not in the bill.
No. If we found any discrimination by any of the companies, after the act had been in operation for a while,, I would be ready to introduce a measure to remedy it.

The minister has forgotten that in the larger Ontario ports the municipalities have police on tihe wharves and boats. That is the case in the Niagara and Toronto districts. Under the Canada Shipping Act and

other legislation the officer commanding the ship, the mate, or other official, is charged with keeping order on the ship. In the city of Toronto the police commissioners, at large cost to the city, have policemen on the ferryboats and other boats, and there have been no complaints in that district, as far as I know.
It may be all very well for the minister to apply this amendment to the ocean ports, but if he applies it to the inland ports he is going to affect the inland trade.

The House in committee of supply, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Department of Marine and Fisheries-Ocean and river service-maintenance and repairs to Dominion steamers and icebreakers, $1,500,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext: This is to provide for the maintenance and operation of the vessels employed on icebreaking service in the St. Lawrence and the gulf, in construction work as required, and in the supply and maintenance of lighthouses, buoys, beacons and similar aids to navigation. All told we have twenty-seven vessels engaged in the service, nineteen on the Atlantic coast and in the St. Lawrence, four on inland waters and four on the Pacific coast.
I see the same amount is proposed this year as was voted last year. Was the expenditure last year up to a million and a half?
For 1925-26 the expenditure was $1,940,000; for 1926-27 up to January 1, it was 11,310,000 odd, and if we bring the figure up to March 31 we will reach the million and a half.

Item agreed to.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
Examination of masters and mates, $20,000.
This is to provide for the examination, and certification of masters and mates.

What about my friend Captain Eden, who gave lectures under this heading for a considerable time at night outside of his business hours and received no remuneration at all, although he put in a claim I think for a few hundred dollars. I understand that those who now give these lectures do so within their working hours.

Item agreed to.
Removal of obstructions in navigable waters, $5,000.

Has any further
consideration been given to the desirability of removing derelicts in harbours? They are the property of some company or individual and there does not seem to be any way by which those who wish to do so can remove them.

If they are an obstruction to navigation the Department of Marine and Fisheries undertakes to remove them and make a claim against the company or person responsible if there is any possibility of enforcing the claim.
Have you ever*succeeded in getting anything under such a claim?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Inspection of live stock shipping, $4,500.
Why the increase-another official?
The increase of $500 is to provide for the salary of an inspector at Halifax, due to the increased shipments through that port.
Does the inspection of live stock come under the Marine and Fisheries department?
No, we inspect only the fittings of the ship.

Item agreed to.
To continue subsidies for wrecking plants-* Quebec and British Columbia, $45,000.
Has any application been made for a subsidy for a wrecking plant between Montreal and lake Ontario?
Not up to the present.
Would it be considered if made?
It certainly would be considered and decided according to its merits.
Why the $10,000 increase?
To increase the subsidy given to the Quebec Wrecking plant?
Why?

We have a contract with the Quebec firm under which we contribute $25,000 to the operation of their equipment. It was represented to the department that they could not meet their obligations, in fact for several years up to 1925-26 their aggregate loss amounted to $142,298- They represented to the department that they could not carry on without an increase of $10,000. Even with the augmented subsidy we do not think they will be able to meet their operating expenses; it will simply help them to reduce the losses.
How many ships do they operate?
They have two powerful vessels with complete wrecking equipment.
Is it a private company?
Yes.

Private companies do not usually carry on under such heavy-losses. It would indicate that there is no necessity for a company of this kind, that there are no wrecks in the river to keep it busy, and that therefore this money had better be saved.	[DOT]
The company is connected with the Canadian Pacific Railway, but is also looking after the wrecks of other companies. This is the only wrecking plant on the St. Lawrence river.
How many wrecks were there last year?
They gave assistance in about fifteen or twenty cases.
Do they secure any salvage money from the owners of the vessels they assist?
Yes, and this is taken into account. At the end of the year if they have made any profit out of the salvage money-plus the subsidy they divide the profit with the department.

Do they keep proper
accounts?

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

Yes, they have to render
accounts to the department.

How much do they
charge per ton for wrecking services?

It depends on the nature
of the work. They cannot have a uniform rate for all cases. I am informed by the deputy that there is something in the contract in regard to it, but unfortunately I have not the document under my hand.

Is any subsidy paid to
wrecking plants in the maritime provinces?
No.
There are no wrecks there.

Some hon. gentleman says
there are no wrecks in the maritimes. He is mistaken. During the season there are wrecks, and the wrecking companies carry on their salvage work. When not so engaged they use their plant for other purposes. They seem to be able to carry on without any subsidy, and I do not see why this company cannot do the same.

If my memory serves me
right, in years past certain wrecking companies were subsidized in the maritime provinces, but the business was not found profitable. The difficulty in granting a subsidy to any wrecking company in the maritime provinces is that there are so many wrecking plants there that we would be flooded with requests for subsidies. Apparently there is enough work in the maritimes for several wrecking plants to operate at a profit.
Is this Quebec company engaged in wrecking work solely?
Yes.

In view of the immense
losses made by this company and the statement of the minister that it expects to make further losses in the future, why does the company continue in business?
The purpose of our contribution is to have the company render efficient service.

But the minister says the
company expects to make losses in the years to come.

This company is to a certain extent connected with the Canadian

Pacific Railway, and looks after their ships, and we are giving this subsidy because it goes to the assistance of the ships of other companies.

There is a dispute between Canada and the United States in regard to the allotment of wave lengths. I understand there are at present about ninety-five different wave lengths of some importance, fifty of them capable of being used for high powered stations and forty-five for rather lower powered stations. Canada has been using exclusively six of these wave lengths on high powered stations and at the same time has been sharing with the United States eleven other wave lengths. During the last few weeks we have been trying to reach an understanding with the United States since they have organized a commission to control broadcasting as we are controlling it in Canada. Prior to not more than two months ago broadcasting in the United States was free; their government had no control at all, and there was what is called pirating of wave lengths.
Since the United States have decided to appoint a commission to control broadcasting as we are controlling it in Canada under the Department of Marine and Fisheries, we have endeavoured to reach an understanding with them and we have claimed twelve wave lengths instead of six out of the ninety-five. We have claimed that we should share fourteen of the less important wave lengths but so far the negotiations have had no satisfactory result. The United States want to discuss the question from a population point of view. Is it the intention of the government to create in the near future a separate portfolio of fisheries? The industry is growing rapidly and it is capable of vast development in the future. If the chairman and members of the Duncan commission, after looking over the Atlantic side of Canada, thought it was necessary to suggest the appointment of a separate deputy, perhaps if they had had occasion to look into [DOT]the conditions at the Pacific coast they would have recommended a separate minister also.

The department has been doing certain work on the bay of Fundy in connection with the removal of obstructions in small streams. At the present time in some of the small rivers running into the bay of Fundy there are obstructions which prevent the salmon proceeding up the river. These small rivers are not and would not be useful for fly fishing nor for the netting of the salmon, but they would be of great value for spawning purposes. The department has been doing certain work in connection with the removal of these obstructions. It is the opinion of many people living in the district whose desire is for the preservation of the salmon and not for the purpose of sport, that the small streams should be preserved so far as possible for spawning. The preservation of the salmon has been rather remarkable. The salmon is holding its own in the bay of Fundy better, I think, than any other fish. At the same time, it is important that we
do our best to help, and here is a means of assisting the continuance of our salmon fishing. While one of the large rivers, the St. John, is the principal source of spawning and of the supply of salmon, it is highly important to have many sources, and therefore I would ask the minister to tell the committee just what is being done in the matter of removing these obstructions in some of the small rivers on the bay of Fundy.

The minister has a considerable number of highly trained men in his department who are engaged in scientific work and who move about the country to a greater or less extent. Now the amount of poaching, and disastrous poaching, that goes on is enormous, especially in the small streams and the spawning grounds. Sometimes it is done by professional poachers; other times by those who have lacked sufficient loyalty to sportsmanlike instincts, but the attitude of the farmers, indeed of the whole people, is not^ sufficiently antagonistic to this poaching. It is with great difficulty that poaching can be prevented simply by overseers or guardians, and I think by stirring up the conscience of the people living in the country a good deal more can be done, because they know that poaching is going on, and if there is an unfriendly attitude towards those who so offend, much good can be gained. Will the minister disclose the policy of the department with regard to reviving the seaplane protection service on the Pacific coast? Members from British Columbia will recall that it was in force two years ago and did excellent service. Those who wish to break the law find it very profitable to go within the prohibited limits, and one guardian with a boat capable of a speed of only five or six miles an hour cannot possibly look after a coast line of fifty or sixty miles, ihe fishing poachers by long experience come to know a boat by the sound of its engine exhaust, and they can tell when the fishery guardian is coming an hour or an hour and a half ahead of his arrival, and this gives them plenty of time to get outside of the protected area. If the patrolman goes north they know for one or two days they are free to poach along the southern shore. Under the seaplane system the poachers would hear the whirr of the plane and within a few minutes it would come over some mountain and land m the sea a few yards ahead of them. As a consequence poaching was very largely stopped. After this system had been in operation for a year a dispute arose between the Naval department and the Marine department on the question of cost, and last year the service was in abeyance, but I remember an assurance being given to this House, in answer to an inquiry by the member for New Westminster, that the service would be reinstated in June-that was last June-under the Marine department. This was not done. We are all in hopes, especially in view of the remarks made in connection with the Imperial conference that Canada is going to take a greater interest in commercial aviation, that this greater interest will be most appropriately displayed in this branch of the service where it is so urgently needed. I believe the seaplane system would be not only more effective but more economical, for unless you [Mr. Hanson.1
put on a whole fleet of boats it is absolutely impossible to protect the mouths of these various rivers from fish poachers. It may be said that this has been done in the past, but conditions have changed in the last few years. To-day there is an enormous market for cheap, inferior fish that were practically unsaleable in former times. It is these fish that I am talking of. They are taken at the mouth of every river and creek, and there is an urgent necessity for their protection because the number of purse seines has increased as much as 400 per cent in certain districts. Therefore it becomes increasingly necessary to preserve the fish or else by and by there will be none to preserve. Some say, do away with purse seines altogether; but this is not always practicable because these fish cannot be taken in gill nets in all waters. My hon. friend from Skeena (Mr. Brady) I know will support me, as did his predecessor who was a Liberal. In his district the only remedy for poaching is for the department to again put the seaplane service in operation. I should like to know from the minister the policy of the department in this regard.
The representations of the hon. gentleman are already known in the department and the matter is at the present time under consideration. I hope a decision will be reached in the course of a few days.
What would be the estimated initial cost of operating two or three seaplanes for one season?

thousand dollars.

I seldom disagree with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) on fishery matters, but I think you would have very much more effective guardianship if you took half that amount of money and placed guardians at the mouths of nearly all these creeks up along the northern coast.
I can claim to be fairly familiar with the conditions there. There are days together when thick fogs and heavy storms prevail. At night time most of the poaching is done, and I do not think that such an expensive service would be justified from Alaska to the northern end of Vancouver island. With respect to the Comox-Alberni coast I am not so familiar of course as is the hon. member, but I think more effective supervision can be exercised by putting good men up there and paying them reasonable wages and supplying them with good boats. The present boats are simply a joke, and the present wages are a tragedy. What can you expect of men in

that northern country if you pay them only $80 or $90 a month for but a part of the year? The remuneration is not sufficient to get dependable men. If you put fifty or sixty men up there and paid them at the rate of $100 a month I think you would get much more effective supervision than by seaplanes. Mr. Chairman, this is a subject of vital importance to the Skeena constituency. I am pleased indeed to see there is to be an increase in the salaries paid overseers. I place great reliance on men of integrity, tact and ability, in other words, men able to resist temptation, than on any other factor in securing effective supervision of our fishing grounds. You will do far more for the protection of your fisheries if you have at the head of the patrol system men who are immune from the many temptations that beset them in their very difficult work. I can vouch for what the hon. member (Mr. Dickie) said regarding salaries paid overseers. There was in the Naas district an overseer of considerable value to the government, a man who was faithful in every possible way. He has left that position. He was married and had two children, and he paid $40 a month in rent. I want to impress upon the minister the fact that out of a salary of $85 a month this man had to pay $4.75 towards superannuation, and that meant a good deal to him. I know that an improvement is being effected in regard to better salaries, but the importance of the patrol system on the Skeena cannot be exaggerated. For those who regard the matter lightly I would point out that this great area comprises five distinct divisions starting at Rivers inlet and going on to Smith's inlet, north to Addenbrook island to Bella Coola, Burke and Dease channels. The central division extends from Namu to Lowe inlet, and in the Skeena division there are Prince Rupert, Skeena river, Chatham sound, Naas river, Port Simpson to the boundary line.
The present patrol system in district number two is hopelessly inadequate. As an illustration of that I might refer the committee to the boats now in use. There is the Cloya, 54 feet long. She is three years old and her rate of travel is seven miles per hour. The Heron is eleven years old, is 45 horse-power, is 58 feet long and travels at eight miles per hour. The Hawk which is twenty years old is 32 feet long and has 14 horse-power. I
computed roughly the obligations in connection with these boats to enable them to cover the area properly. It would be absolutely necessary for each of them to cover 200 miles per day, and inasmuch as they have to stop vessels for examination, which takes time, it necessarily follows that they must be properly equipped in the matter of speed. I would urge the minister to place in that district up to date patrol boats capable of a speed of fifteen miles per hour. They should have accommodation for four persons with extra accommodation for the officials.
I shall say just one word now in regard to aeroplanes. Though at first it was considered that the aeroplane might have met all the exigencies which it was called upon to meet,
I do not think it does so to the extent suggested by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill). Aeroplanes cannot operate successfully in cloudy, foggy weather, and most of the poaching is done on obscure days when the visibility is poor. A good deal of it takes place also at night. The aeroplane cannot meet these requirements completely, and though the government may consider the advisability of using them, I, still stress the importance of an efficient 'boat patrol. You want men as well as boats; the boats are essential 'but you cannot dispense with well trained men. So important is this fishing business to Canada that I am pleased to know that the government and particularly the minister is going the right way about it by providing up-to-date boats and, better still, men whose appointment will not be due to political pull. These men have charge of what may be considered' a sacred treasure and if we did nothing else than provide for this great industry men of integrity we should be doing a good deal for the Dominion. Overseers should be given good wages so as to be removed from the sphere of temptation. I urge the minister to see to it that an up-to-date patrol system is put into operation in district No. 2 and wherever our fisheries demand them. Most important of all is it to pay the men good salaries. Just imagine a man engaged on these rough waters from morning till night from one end of the week to the other receiving a salary which any girl working in the post office on stated hours is paid-$85 a month. That is what the overseers in my constituency receive. I am pleased to learn that the minister and the Marine department are alive to the importance of good overseers, and I would ask him to have guardians placed at the mouth of the more important creeks in district No. 2 and along the whole coast.

I must congratulate the minister upon the economy he has displayed in the conduct of his department. That economy has not been evident in any of the other departments of government because I have observed that in the case of every other department thousands and tens of thousands- may I say hundreds of thousands?-are being wasted; money is being spent without sufficient justification for the expenditure. But when it comes to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, so vitally important to my province and the maritime provinces generally, I notice that they are very anxious to keep down the expenditure. I must congratulate the minister upon that but I wish the heads of other departments would take a leaf out of his book and practise greater economy until we have succeeded in reducing our public debt. Until that time comes let them go very carefully in the matter of increasing the amount of their estimates.

Mr. R(^S (Kingston); I think the really important subject with which this department has to deal is the development of fish culture. Some three years ago I made some remarks on the subject and I should like to follow up those remarks, especially in view of the fact that in the Montreal Daily Star of April 11, 1925, there is an item headed as follows:
A half century of waste.
The article begins as follows:
After carrying on fish hatcheries for half a century the federal Department of Marine and Fisheries is now starting an investigation and series of experiments to find out whether after all it is worth while.
This is very much in line with the criticism which I will make and which, I hope, will be constructive and not destructive with relation to the work of the department. For years we have known in different parts of this country that fry and fingerlings have been put into the waters of rivers and lakes from which we have never seen one of these fish caught. It is quite true that in some parts the work has been successful, but I know of many places where there has been a lack o/ success and there is surely some reason for that. This subject was taken up by a section of the research council known as the biological board. These men made investigations, the result of which proved what many people had surmised, namely, that in many cases the fish culture had been successful as regards the development of fingerlings and fry; in other words that the hatchery had been successful in the development of these small fish, but that care had not been taken in the selection of waters and that consequently thousands of dollars under this vote had been absolutely wasted. This work was placed under the biological board which, I think in 1923, was put under the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
In order to show the necessity for this work I should state that during 1920 a report -had been made in regard to lobster canning along the -coast of the maritime provinces. A certain defect had arisen there in regard to lobster canning and the industry was suffering very much from it. A report was made that this was largely due to insanitary conditions. It was fairly well accepted that this might be the cause of a great deal of the trouble in this regard. However we find that in the following year there was still evidence of very unsatisfactory conditions prevailing. In fact in spite of the report of the biological board or the scientific men who were taking up this



Supply-Marine and Fisheries
work, we found that the questio^ of sanitation was being absolutely neglected! The 1922 report states:
I regret very much to have to report that over 75 per cent of the lobster canners still continue to violate one or more of the fundamental laws of sanitary science.
The final clause reads:
The conditions in and arou-nd factories as recorded in my report for 1920 are almost exactly the conditions recorded in 1921.
The object of the board was to standardize this work to produce a standard system of sanitation around these canning factories. The result was that whenever an attempt was made to put this into force, the large factories would refuse to do so because the smaller ones were not doing it. Some of the smaller ones went out of business because they were forced to put some more money into their factories.
After the biological board was incorporated in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, the matter was followed up. Two stations were formed and three principles were to mark the work of those two stations. The method was to apply scientific principles to fish culture. At the head of the board there was Doctor Knight who had a great deal of experience in biological work. That gentleman is no longer on the board; he has resigned, and now I come to what I consider is the important thing. His resignation was made with the intention of securing better results in the department. I hope the minister will take the criticism which I am going to make as being of a constructive nature and that the treatment which Doctor Knight received will not be received by the gentleman who has replaced him.
The cause of Doctor Knight's resignation was distinctly want of cooperation between officials of the department and the biological board. That want of cooperation is exemplified in the class that will be held at Truro. To go back, let me say that the object of the research council is to develop a class of scientific research men in all departments in this country. The biological board set itself to the task of developing the present officials into some kind of scientific investigators, but it found that it could not go ahead owing to lack of data, and that the data could be gathered only by scientific operators or officials. The board decided to open up these classes and to bring the officials to them so that they could give them some instruction in this scientific work. It is quite true that many of these officials met in this class, but they exercised a passive resistance to the work. It
I Mr. A. E. Ross.]
may.be quite true that the work at first may be a little heavy, a little beyond their grasp, but in time, just as the prospector in our mining fields has become an expert in his work, so these officials would gradually become experienced, so far as you can make them, along scientific lines.
The point is that in this .work the department permitted a condition characterized by an absolute want of cooperation to exist, so much so that Doctor Knight felt called upon to resign. Now that this department is being reorganized and put under a new method of administration, I would like to draw the attention of the department to the fact that they must realize that advance in fish culture, in the whole fishing industry, will be developed by the study of these scientific men. That is the object of the research council, and if the department does not cooperate with it, these men, scientific men as they are, must drop out and leave. They have been given a fairly good start and I believe progress can be made with better cooperation.
I went up the Pacific coast to Alaska and I visited some twenty to twenty-two canneries on that coast. I was amazed at the degree of sanitation that prevailed around an industry of that kind, because any person who has gone into a cannery and watched the operation of bringing these fish from the sea, cleaning them and putting them into the cans, will understand that it is a difficult matter to adhere to sanitary methods. I was absolutely amazed to find that in all of these twenty-two canneries they had developed sanitary methods. In all the canneries I visited I found only one person handling the fish with bare hands. All the other employees in all these canneries were handling the fish with gloves, and were dressed in absolutely sanitary costumes. When you come to the Atlantic coast and deal with the matter of lobster curing, there is far more reason for sanitary methods there, because the anatomical features of this fish make it very difficult to prevent the tearing of the intestinal tract, causing the development of bacteria, and so on. These investigators and inspectors would find that after the lobster had1 been boiled and prepared for canning, instead of being put into the can at once, it would be left out for some hours during the day or perhaps left out over night. The fishing industry in Canada is now a large one, and it is a matter of importance to us that the canning should be done along sanitary lines and according to scientific methods. I trust now that the matter has been brought to the attention of the minister and the department, in view of the fact that

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
we are going to have a new adbainistration in connection with fishery matters-I am not censuring anybody, because I know that this work must be carried on under men equipped with scientific knowledge-that we shall hear of great progress in the future. The success of this industry means a lot to Canada. If our canning is not satisfactory and our canned fish is not acceptable to the retail trade, the industry suffers because of its reputation. I would like to be assured that the department will be more active in. cooperating in these matters in the future. If some official stands in the way of cooperation, I believe that the industry as greater than the official, and he must be given to understand that in this as in all other matters science is going to play its part, and no official can stand in the way and block it.
I may say that the closest cooperation does exist at the present time between all the officers of the department and the board,

I thought the minister might say that, yet here is a motion passed by the research committee in 1925. I tried to get the report for 1926, but could not. The motion reads:
That the committee believes that the cooperation set forth in resolution 3, meeting of the executive committee of the board for January 3, 1925, has not been freely given, and desires to so report to the executive committee.

May I ask what encouragement is being given by the department to the average citizen who is interested in the development of our fisheries, particularly the salmon and trout industries? I know of a man in Nova Scotia who is very much interested in the culture of salmon and trout, and who has as a result several year's work established, something along the line of hatcheries for the development of the ova and the fish fry. He appeared before the officials of the department and asked to be allowed to give a demonstration. No doubt one of the deputies will remember the case. This man's name is Parry. He was asked to take his plant over to St. John, New Brunswick, but owing to pecuniary circumstances he has not been able to follow that up. He did remove the plant over there, but was not given the opportunity of supervising the working of the plant. I would point out to the minister and his deputy that it is .in the interests of this country to encourage in every possible way men of this kind who are willing to volunteer their services and information for the development of our fisheries. I ask from the department, their earnest consideration for 32649-139J
such men as Mr. Parry, who are willing and ready to give their knowledge and their services to the department for the encouragement of the fish industry. I think there should be some financial assistance given to such men. We vote money to help the farmers and to encourage different industries throughout the country. Why should we not encourage such men as the one I have mentioned, who is interested in the development of the fisheries of this country? I would like to have a statement from the minister. Does he know of this case?

We know of Mr. Parry,
and I am informed by the director of fisheries that he has been told that we were quite ready to provide the necessary facilities to make a trial of his method. We are doing the same thing in regard to everyone who is in a position to offer any valuable new suggestion. The department is always ready to receive new suggestions and to give them every consideration.

I quite appreciate that, but this gentleman happens to be a poor apple orchardist in Kings county, and in the last two or three years the fruit industiy has not been very successful, and he has not made much money. His time is taken up largely with the development of his orchard, and I understand that he cannot afford to lose the time and money in going over there to supervise the wrorking of his plant. I ask the minister to take that into consideration, and to see if it would not be possible to allow this gentleman something for the loss of his time when engaged on a work that is for the benefit of Canada.

I fully approve of this
vote. I expect that a small portion of it at least will go to the province of British Columbia. I know they are carrying on excellent work in that province. There is just one matter on which I wish to question the minister; it is a matter I have already discussed with the department, and that is the question of restocking some of the rivers on the lower mainland near the international boundary in the province of British Columbia. I believe that there is some objection on the part of the department to restocking these rivers with certain kinds of game fish, such as cut-throat and speckled trout. The department consider that they could safely, in the interest of salmon culture, restock these streams with stee'lhead, and it was indicated that it would be possible to hatch this species

of trout in the hatcheries in that vicinity. I would like to know if provision is being made under this vote for something along that line.
I am informed that the matter is in hand and will be provided for next year.
That is in the fall of 1927?
