speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: The reason of the increase is that there have been actually organized, but not authorized, some forty-nine cadet units which have been functioning without any assistance from the department, and the amount of $100,000 will not very much more than take care of them. I will give the hon. member the number of these units and the provinces in which they are located.
We shall be very glad to have that.
Four in Alberta, four in British Columbia, two in Manitoba, one in New Brunswick, five in Nova Scotia, fifteen in Ontario, sixteen in Quebec and two in Saskatchewan.

I understand they are having province-wide shooting contests. Someone was telling me that where one boy won a contest he was chosen to compete against a boy from another town, and finally it came to be a province-wide contest. What does the minister know about these contests?
]Mr. ' Barber.]

There is a contest in which these teams participate. Scores are kept, and the contest is for a trophy presented by His Majesty. The South African boys won the contest for the last two years, and I think the Canadian boys were second.

I have always been opposed to the military authorities having any influence on the educational system of the different provinces. Other Dominion departments do not interfere with the matter of education in the provinces. The provinces themselves are supposed to control education, and I am therefore opposed to the increase of $100,000 in the cadet vote, which increase is evidently due to the number of units that are being asked for. I believe cadet training is military training. It is supervised by the Department of National Defence and is paid for by that department. It certainly was the idea of the founder, Sir Frederick Borden, to build up a citizen soldiery. Up till now, as I said a moment ago, the vote has been $400,000. To-day $100,000 is to be added, and the total of $500,000 I believe will be supplemented by the Strath-cona trust fund. Possibly the minister could tell us what will be contributed by that trust fund.
The Strathcona trust fund is $500,000, the interest on which is available for the giving of prizes to cadets in the various provinces. The money is distributed on the basis of the school population.

In its issue of February 24, 1927, the Ottawa Journal very clearly pointed out that cadet training is military in character. It said:
If Agnes Maephail M.P., doesn't understand the purpose of high school cadets, and the need of men of courage who can shoot straight, the white women in Shanghai do.
I thank the Journal for that item. I think the newspaper is right and that cadet training is military training. I have always maintained this because I cannot imagine the Department of National Defence asking for a vote of half a million dollars and going to the trouble of having provincial contests, training officers, and providing uniforms and arms unless the organization was entirely military in character.
To defend the women of Canada and every other country.
That is an old joke. Nobody believes that any more.

It is no joke, it is an absolute fact.

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services

The purpose of cadets, then, is to produce men who can shoot straight; or to state it more brutally, to teach the boys of Canada to be "killers of men." I think anyone who has watched cadets training before these buildings could hardly deny the fact that cadet training is military training. Every time the militia troops parade, to receive military visitors or at military funerals and displays, the cadets take part, clearly identifying themselves with the military machine. Military men train them. The Department of National Defence pays the bill. We can safely conclude that cadet training is military training.
The Teachers' Journal in an issue of a few years ago told of cadet reviews in military barracks in Winnipeg at which winning teams of school cadets took 28 to 34 seconds respectively to bring machine guns into action. The same journal states that teachers in military district No. 10 would get free transportation and subsistence while taking the cadet officers' training course in Tuxedo barracks, Winnipeg. Two years ago the Minister of National Defence assured us it was true that the instructor of cadets received two dollars per head for each cadet up to fifty, and one dollar per head for each cadet over that number. It is easy to see how the larger salary paid the instructor will make him a good recruiting officer, and how a boycott against boys not in the corps can be effectively used, and I believe is used, to swell the number of cadets.
There are many people whose boys are taking cadet training who say:	It's just
physical training. This, I believe, is an error, and if to-day I can but establish in the minds of even some Canadian parents that cadet training is not physical but military training, I shall think it worth while to make this effort. The development of a healthy body, if considered at all, is considered only as a means to an end in military training, not as an end in itself. The aim is to make soldiers out of boys. Men who have specialized in physical training affirm that military drill is not good physical training. Dudley A. Sargent, physical instructor of Harvard, physical instructor and medical doctor, -has said:
Taking the most favourable view possible of military drill as a physical exercise, we are led to conclude that its strained positions and closely localized movements do not afford the essential requisites for developing the muscles and improving respiration and circulation, thereby improving the general health and condition of the system.
Let me quote now from an extract taken from the Boston Medical and Surgical Journal:
This defect, we are pleased to state, is recognized by the great military nations of Europe, and measures are taken to give all the recruits from three to twelve months gymnastic training to develop them as men before they are expected to conform to the requirements of the soldier.
I could quote many other authorities to the same effect, but I will give only one more. Mr. Claxton, former United States Commissioner of Education, said:
All schools should provide such means of physical culture through outdoor games and exercises as will result in the best possible control of the body and all its members. I do not believe that military drill in our public schools is the best means to this end and I feel quite certain that rifle practice in the schools is undesirable. There is so much else that is better for all purposes that can be provided at much less cost.	,
During the war "setting up" exercises were freely used to counteract the bad results of military drill. I believe all military schools employ physical training in order to keep their men fit. In games, in the gymnasium and on the track boys and girls dress for vigorous exercise. They aim, one might say, to get up a sweat; but cadets go out in stiff-looking, warm clothing and carry heavy guns, and they have all the appearance of trying to keep cool. I believe that our youth, both" boys and girls, need physical training, but that training should be of the kind that is pleasing to them. To be good physical training it should be something which in itself is so pleasing that those engaged in it become intensely interested. Let me quote John Langdon-Davies of England on this point. In his book, A Public School in War Time, I find the following at page nine:
Physical training which is to form character must appeal to the child as a pleasure. A pleasant thing is one which appeals to healthy instincts, and this can never be the case of routine drill. This last has to rely on something else than healthy pleasure for its incentives, thus proving itself to be the bending of human nature out of its natural course for the sake of an external object, and is therefore the antithesis of education.
I should like to make it clear that it is not the sum of money involved that I am objecting to. I would favour a sum exceeding the amount now in the estimates, to be paid by the Department of Health to the Department of Education in the various provinces for them to use for physical training, but not for military training. I think we could safely model our physical training on

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
the Swedish system. We should use the beauty of colour, music and form in training youth physically, but all military forms should be eliminated.
We know Sweden leads the world1 in physical training. As a matter of fact, in no other country have results been so striking, and she sticks to her athletic sports and games and does not indulge at all in military training. Is it not strange that Canada is increasing the military training of cadets at this time? I see no cause for it. I fail to understand why a department of the Dominion government is inducing the boys of Canada to take miltary training. France, after the crushing defeat of 1871 began to train her school boys to the practice of arms, but in 1890, after fifteen years experience, she abandoned the cadet system, not because the problem of defence was less urgent, but because military training was arresting the physical development of her secondary schoolboys. Australia tried the military system of training, but previous to the war her director general, after a thorough study of the problem in Switzerland, Sweden, Germany, France and England, recommended a system of games and organized athletic sports as the best training for schoolboys. I might quote other countries, but I will leave it there.
John Stuart Mill has said that all attempts by the state to bias the conclusions of its subjects on disputed points are evil. And that is just what the state is doing by influencing the education of the provinces. Education is being used as a political institution to form habits of thought and to circumscribe knowledge in such a way as to make one set of opinions inevitable. That is my greatest objection to military training The thing it does to the boy's mind is far more disastrous than the injury it does to his body. A great educationist, Mr. J. L. Paton, headmaster of Manchester grammar school writes:
The people who instil military training permanently into our schools seem to me to be closing the gates of hope upon mankind.
These are very strong words coming from a great educationist. When in Canada not long ago he said practically the same thing. Bertrand Russell has said:
I think it would be a real gain if men could be made to see that militarism is a form of cowardice. It is a desire for security that makes the common man acquiesce in the schemes of the militarists. Armaments are the most foolish method imaginable for seeking security, but fear makes men unable to think clearly and so they cling to old absurdities.
Miss Macphail.]
In our own families, as every one of us knows, active goodwill is the central principle that keeps the unit together, and that is true of our schools and of every form of government. It is true of every form of group life. If we have not active goodwill there can be no real progress. The world stands today in need of that spirit and, laugh me to scorn if you will, I think it is the only road to security. We cannot find security by arming ourselves to the very limit. I do not believe that preparedness for war will bring peace. What we carefully prepare for we usually get. If we prepare for war we get war; if we prepare for peace we shall get peace.

Were we prepared for war
in 1914, either .in Canada or in Great Britain?

Great Britain, I think,
had been carefully preparing for war for a long time. She was not as unprepared as we have been led to believe. To my mind cadet training is the most vicious part of our national defence scheme. I have never attacked a permanent army if other people want that sort of thing, but I do object to imposing upon boys our own ideas instead of letting them think for themselves. I do not believe in imposing the thoughts of age upon the mind of youth. If we do not know the way out let us keep it to ourselves. Let us give the boys a chance to come to their own conclusions.
We may safely conclude that war settles nothing. It causes other wars by arousing hatreds. It brings unemployment, poverty, misery, crime and death. We can call as witnesses to this truth Viscount Grey, Lloyd George, Earl Haig, Sir Ian Hamilton, Wilson, Ponsonby, Morel, Sir Arthur Currie and a score of others. I will ndtjtire the House by citing further authorities but they are innumerable. Yet military training in the schools leads the youth to think of it as the one method of settling international disputes. Military training is one of the ways of capturing the schools and colleges for the old philosophy. And it works. The militarist knows that all the talk about peace conferences, world courts and leagues of nations will fall on deaf ears if he can instil the war psychology into the minds of our youth. A boy who is trained in military methods will naturally think of war the moment trouble arises.
In the stone age men made use of brute force when groups quarrelled. We have progressed far since then. Surely no one in this House, even the most ardent Tory, will suggest for a moment that we have not moved

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
forward considerably since the stone age. We live in a scientific age and our knowledge is vast. Great numbers of inventions, coupled with the sciences, have revolutionized our methods of living, but we still use force as the means of settling international disputes. Science has made war much more destructive than it was in the distant past, and it will be still more terrible in the future. Yet war is an institution which is mothered by the state and sanctioned by the church.
Not all the churches.

No not all; most of
them. Around war has been woven romance and adventure, beauty of form, colour and sound. It has been given a greater place in song and story than any other one theme. But we know that it is a grinning demon. We know that it has neither glory nor beauty. The best literature of to-day is almost a unit in denouncing war. Wars are now world-embracing, and civilization can stand few more of them. It is more than likely that it would find it impossible to stand one more. Would it not be more sensible to leave the minds of youth free to study the causes of war and the means of removing those causes? The Women's International League for Peace on July, 1926, in convention in Dublin put themselves on record as follows:
We women of the W.I.L. are of the opinion that the time has come to educate all children for peace; we hold it to be a crime against the souls of ripening youth to picture war to them as a necessity, or even as a moral duty; to train them in war-handicraft and instruct them in the art of killing. We consider the present-day militarization of youth to be a vestige of barbarism; and that this militarization takes place simultaneously with the convening of disarmament conferences and court of arbitration proceedings, rvith the assurance of the "Locarno Peace spirit", we hold to be one of the greatest hypocrisies in the history of mankind.
That resolution does not overstate it. I am often led to wonder how Christian nations can find comfort for their consciences in the wholesale slaughter of human life. The soul of every one of us here to-day revolts at the thought of murder, but soars in ecstasy if the murder be multiplied sufficiently to be called war. Wars are fought to gain markets, to extend territory, to increase investments, to protect property, to procure some necessary raw product. For instance, we fight to secure oil in order that we may have oil to fight with. I do not think that can be doubted. There is more fuss about oil now than about any other one thing. We must therefore conclude that civilization values property above human
life. Fear is one cause of war and fear can be largely eliminated by early training. Military training in the schools thrives on fear and produces it. Military training in schools creates a bombastic military spirit of toy soldierism. Here is a picture of cadets parading, preparing for the annual review on Empire day, and among them there are three little chaps, little drummers, three of the youngest drummers in the massed bugle band. Reading from left to right they are:
William Wilkinson, of Fern Avenue school, aged six years.
Chester Mueller, of Kent school, aged five years.
Thomas Martin, of Park school, aged seven years.
Some returned soldier sent me this dipping and he had written in pencil at the top, with a dart pointing towards the little chaps:
Over in Germany they teach the children to be soldiers, so we were told in 1914. In Canada we wait until they are grown up.
I do not know how any of you can get any pleasure out of thinking that boys of five, six and seven years were parading with bands, deeming themselves soldiers. But there is certainly no comfort in it for me.
The number of cadets has very largely increased. The minister proved that by showing that they need $100,000 to take care of new units.	I have not the figures for the
year ending March 31st, 1926, but for the year ending March 31st, 1925, there were 40,686 more cadets in Canada than there were in the year 1920. That is to say the number of cadets increased in five years by 40,686, the greatest increase taking place in Quebec and Ontario-and I would not like to say that the best thought of Canada is in those provinces, much as I would like to do so. There is world-wide movement against war, and particularly against militarizing the mind of youth. The youths of Germany, of France, of England, of the United States-in fact of any country you can name-have risen in revolt against being harnessed by the military powers. They are sick of it. They see that the thing has not led them anywhere. In Canada too we have heard among our people some indications of a revolt against militarism. In that connection I suppose the labour movement in Canada should be given first place; it certainly should have that position throughout the world. Not only is labour opposed to militarism but the farmers are also. The same feeling is evident among women's organizations like the National Council of Women and the organizations which represent the more advanced

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
thought on this question, like the Women's International League for Freedom, and the Christian Student movement. There are not, I believe, in Canada, any International War Resisters. The Teachers' International Federation, which is to meet in July of this year in Toronto, is to discuss the elimination of militarism from among our school children. Canada has not taken as forward a step in the matter of discarding the military machine as some countries have, possibly because we have not suffered as much from war as some other countries, and do not know from actual experience how terrible it is. But there are some gleams of light even here. In the province of British Columbia last year-and they are preparing again for the event this year-many of the schools observed a "good-will day" on May 18th. That day was decided upon by the Teachers' Federation as the day on which the school children of the country should express what thoughts they had on good-will. This year, I am very glad to say, the city of Winnipeg has consented* to the schools of that city also observing the goodwill day on May 18th. The Winnipeg Tribune had a very interesting editorial on the matter quite recently, pointing out the need for celebrations of the kind. Children going to school should learn that the world is a much smaller place than it used to be, and that the children of all countries ought to be good friends and neighbours. But the lessons on that subject should not be limited to one day in the year. More frequent lessons would impress the subject on their minds more indelibly.
Resolutions have been passed by numerous public bodies in Canada in opposition to military training. For that reason I wondered why the vote for this purpose was increased at this particular time. Even in the city of Toronto the Ontario Educational Association passed two or three resolutions condemning military training and any teaching of a warlike spirit in the schools. A couple of years ago a survey was made of the public school system in British Columbia by two educationalists, Doctor Putman of Ottawa, and Dr. George Weir of the university of British Columbia. On page 95 of their report they say this in regard to military training:
We take strong exception to the plan of having any part of this work-
Speaking of organized play and supervised games-
-done by militia officers, who naturally give it a military bent.
Miss Macphail.l
Then on page 396 they say:
We think the schools would suffer no real loss if every vestige of military training were eliminated from the school program.
I think the Prime Minister received a letter dated February 28th, 1927, from the Trades and Labour Council of Calgary, protesting against this increase in military training, and against the increased expenditure for national defence. That letter was signed by J. E. Young, secretary of the council. The Saskatchewan school trustees held a convention in Moose Jaw on February 16, 17 and 18, of the present year and resolution No. 19 passed by them was in effect as follows:
We are opposed to the war propaganda, individualism and competition that we are teaching in our schools; and we go on record as being in favour of changing our history books and readers, and the teaching of peace and cooperation.
The students of the university of British Columbia revolted at military training in that institution. There was some talk about military training being made compulsory in the university, and an editorial appeared in the university paper taking a very strong stand against it. It declared:
There has never been any wholehearted attempt to make militarists out of the students here, since the war, for the simple reason that the returned men at this college would not stand for it. Now that practically all of them have graduated, the tom-tom is beginning to beat once more.
It is quite evident that the students of that university are against allowing themselves to be driven where the military machine wants them to go. The Board of Education of Cleveland, according to the Christian Science Monitor, in its issue of January 13, 1926, came out in favour of eliminating cadet training from their curriculum, and it was to become effective last June.
I have not made any real' attempt to gather all the protests that have been made against militarism or military training, but 1 have quoted sufficient to show that in Canada, indeed on the North American continent, there is a great body of public opinion in revolt against military training for our young people. It is evident that youth itself is in revolt against many old time institutions and customs, and they are very much in revolt against war. Speaking figuratively we can look upon Canada as a youth. When this nation is compared with other nations of the world, it is a very youthful one indeed. Such being the case, Canada should take its place in the ranks of those who have risen against war and all that it means. I ask against what enemies are we preparing the

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
youth of our country to fight? Apparently we have no enemies. Therefore I should say that Canada is in an ideal position to lead the world towards other methods of settling international disputes.
If one-half of the things'that we hear about Canada being an autonomous, self-governing nation are true, we are not going to be embroiled in all the wars of the continent of Europe. We live on the continent of North America, and it does not look as though we are going to have any enemy against which we need arm ourselves. The only one that I can think of is the United States, and we would have a tremendous time arming ourselves against the United States should they want to annex us, which I do not believe they want to do. Some one in conversation said to me just the other day: Why should we sit still and accept the protection of the United States? I say: Why should we not?
I think we should take advantage of every position which is naturally ours.
I wish the parliament of Canada could for five minutes view this question of militarizing the minds of youth as I view it. If you want to train grown men to be soldiers, you can do so; they are grown up and they know what they want to do; but leave the boys alone. I wish the people would say to the Department of National Defence and the government: Take your hands off the schoolboys of Canada. That is all I am asking the government to do. If they want to increase their military appropriations in other directions, I do not suppose we shall be able to prevent it. I do not know whether it is true that about 40 per cent of the expenditure of Canada goes for wars, past, present and future; but if it is true, it is a terrific waste of money; it is far too much money. It is much more than the thing is worth, and if we would spend that amount of money in making life better for the people who are alive rather than in attempting to kill somebody, we would have gone a long way towards eliminating the causes of war.
I do not intend to detain the committee any longer. I will say once more to the government: If you are paying for the instruction of the men who train cadets; if you are buying the uniforms; if you are supplying the guns; if you are giving the prizes which I think it is said were given by His Majesty- at any rate somebody is giving them and I suppose the people of some country are paying for them-if you are doing everything you can to induce these boys to take military training against their own inclination-because
I do not think the boys are very enthusiastic about it-you cannot wonder the number of units is increasing all the time. All I can say is that this expenditure will increase as time goes on, and the result will be that the minds of the boys in Canada will be biased while they are growing up and they will look upon war as the only method of settling international disputes. Because I do not believe it is the best method and because I think the government is doing the boys of Canada the greatest possible injustice it can do to them,
I move that this item be reduced by $499,999.

This is the first occasion on
which I feel it incumbent upon me to object to the observations made by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail). This is the. first time that I find myself in utter opposition to any hon. member in the presentation of matters to this House. On the question of cadet training, I can present to the hon. member for Southeast Grey an experience of twenty-eight years in cadet work, not merely in Canada, but in Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. Tennyson once said: "Self-knowledge, self-reverence and selfcontrol are the three great powers in the development of character and morality," and in cadet training we have taught and inculcated that in a degree which is perhaps not known by the hon. member but is known by all who have seen the effects of cadet training in the high schools and particularly in high schools throughout Canada.
I am sorry to have absolutely to oppose the views of the hon. member. I would like to be able to agree with her, but in a question of this sort we must be honest and we must recognize the fact that there is nothing military in the training given to-day to cadets in the high schools of this country. Furthermore the physical training is absolutely up to date and commensurate with the best improvements in the physical development of our youth. I would ask any hon. member just to ponder over this question: What is the purpose and aim of the educators of our youth in Canada to-day? It is this: To make good citizens; to make law-abiding citizens, to make citizens who will live up to their responsibilities. I say unhesitatingly and without fear of contradiction that cadet training in our schools to-day is bringing out from our youth all those attributes of honour, discipline and self-control that go to make a great country and a great nation.
Furthermore it is wrong, it is, to say the least, improper, that a viewpoint is given out to our people and to this House that our
Supply-Defence-Cadet Services

youth are made biased by the training which they receive in those schools. I would like the hon. member for Southeast Grey to visit the schools in British Columbia andi see the actual conditions and the teachers who have charge of those boys. I would challenge her to see even a semblance, even a very shadow, of that military dragon which she has lifted up and presented to many people who are ignorant of the facts that lie behind this cadet training.

Perhaps the hon.
gentleman has not read the report to which the hon. member for Southeast Grey has referred, namely, an inquiry into conditions in the schools in British Columbia, in which report the commissioners spoke very strongly against the cadet training.

I had a part in the report of that commission. I likewise assisted in a small way in the work of the commission. Whether that report was adverse or not, you will always have opinions adverse to every scheme that has as its foundation the purpose of ennobling our youth and making them law-abiding citizens.

I hope the hon.
member does not suggest that Doctor Putman and the other commissioner were opposed.

I am quite pleased when
I hear the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre refer to Doctor Putman. I know him personally. Of course, in any scheme, no matter what it is, there are imperfections, and he may have instanced a few things that perhaps he would like to see improved, but I say unhesitatingly that if fiere is one thing that has been for the goo( of Canada, it is the cadet training that is carried on in the high schools of the Dominion, and I say that that training should be continued until there is not one boy in the length and breadth of Canada who will not know how to stand up straight and control his body as well as his mind. That is the purpose of cadet training. Everybody knows that the newspapers to-day are full of instances showing how our youth are undisciplined and unwilling to accept authority. They want to go the wild and easy way. I say that there is no form of moral discipline more natural in its application and more worthy of commendation than the cadet training that is given in the high schools of British Columbia; I cannot speak for the other provinces.
As to handling a rifle, you would imagine from all this talk about shooting, that every boy is being taught to prepare for the day

when he may point that weapon directly towards the enemy. That is not so. I will tell you why we are teaching the boys to shoot. There is not a season in which we have not scores of deaths through negligence and lack of knowledge of handling a rifle. By our cadet training we have reduced to a minimum the number of accidents in the hunting field in British Columbia. We teach the boy that in order to shoot well he must have perfect control over his muscles, that his brain and body must coordinate perfectly.
I say that it is absolutely necessary that our boys be trained in the use of the rifle, not for military purposes by any means. I wish that those who are antagonistic to cadet training would only do the intelligent thing and go and visit the schools where this training is being carried on before they oppose it. I am speaking from experience, and I am very sorry indeed that I should be called upon to protest strongly against what I consider the exaggerated picture of cadet training that has been presented by the hon. member for Southeast Grey. I say that if we had more of this training, we would have less crime, and we would have a better direction of the energy of our youth into proper channels.

There are a few '
remarks that I should like to make with regard to this general question. I feel sorry in some ways that we have in the present Minister of National Defence a gentleman whom I think we all very highly respect. It makes it perhaps a little more difficult to speak against his estimates, but I am quite sure that none of us here thinks that when an hon. member speaks against these estimates he is speaking against any individual. I should also like to make it very clear that when we speak against militarism, we are not in any way making light of thofee who very sincerely think that that is the best way of defending their country. But we do say that there are other ways, as we see it, and we hope that our friends who differ from us will at least do us the courtesy of thinking that we are not doing this simply because we are cowards or because we have no love for our country.
I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Southeast Grey on her very excellent presentation of this case. I do not wish to make a speech of any length, because all I could do would be to endorse what she has already said so well. I would, however, like to congratulate the women of Canada upon having sent as their first representative to this par-

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
liament one who has. taken such forward ground with regard to a great problem of this character.	*
No.

Someone says no.
I quite recognize that there are differences of opinion. hilst we may have considered that in the past it was by force of arms we would best be able to protect our country, the war has taught a very large number of people that war is absolutely futile in settling any question whatever. I know that there are a large number of people in 'Canada who believe that. Perhaps they have not had the opportunity of voicing their sentiments as freely as I do; perhaps some are a little bit loath to voice their sentiments, but there are a large number of people in this country who are thinking along these lines. We do not stand alone in this. Reference has been made to the labour movement. Tens of thousands of labour men went overseas and fought in the war, and the Trades and Labour Congress has endorsed this movement. The Canadian Council of Agriculture, representing the great farm movement in this country, has also endorsed it, as well as a number of the churches. The United church, for instance, has passed this question of cadet training to all its courts, and it is now being discussed from coast to coast. More than that, I would point out that a large number of our younger men, headed by those who were themselves at the front, have decided that they cannot hope for any good result from any war in the future, and they are looking to some peaceful way of settling troubles in the days to come.
Perhaps we might have been prepared for some exhibition of militarism for some little time after the war. Long after a storm has ceased to blow we know that the waves run high, but after a while they 'begin to subside, and I had hoped that the military feeling would gradually subside as we got away from the war. Unfortunately, however, the increased estimates before us would seem to show that the forces that would carry on our affairs along the old lines are very strong indeed, and one of the greatest troubles about this military question is that we have professional militarists whose job is involved, men who are at the thing in season and out, trying in every way to use their influence to perpetuate it. They may be quite honest and sincere in their viewpoint. I am not suggesting that they are not, but they are professional militarists; in season and out of season they are pressing this matter, and the great mass
of public opinion has no very easy way of manifesting itself. I should like to ask the minister if some time in the course of this debate he will be good enough to answer the question which I asked his predecessor and to which I received no answer, that is, against whom are we arming? With regard to any expenditure that is proposed the minister is expected to state its purpose. With regard to military matters the minister merely gives us in this case the specific purpose for which the expenditure is asked, but he does not state the great objective of the whole of the military estimates and expenditures. I ask, against whom are we arming? It is unthinkable that we could ever hope to fight the United States. I cannot think that after the last European war it is possible for Canadians to be dragged into another European war. I cannot think that we are going to travel over the Pacific to get into trouble in Asia. No country is more favourably situated than Canada for being in the forefront in a great peace movement. We have everything to gain by such a movement and nothing to lose. So far as external enemies are concerned, will the minister tell us definitely against whom we are arming? Some people have said; that we are arming against the radicals in this country. I cannot believe that that statement was made seriously. Are we proposing to settle questions of domestic trouble by means of force? It seems to me we are surely in a position where we can remove causes of friction or misunderstanding in some other way. I cannot think that our Canadian people are going to be militarized to that extent. Against whom are we arming?	*
What is the cause of our great security at the present time?
Somebody suggests war weariness, that is part of it. It is because we are not an aggressive nation. No one wants to attack us and we do not want to attack anyone.
The answer is that Great Britain is armed to the teeth and prepared to protect her possessions overseas as well as her home shores.
I quite believe that that is the common position taken by many, but I do not believe it is a correct one. I do not believe that we are one bit safer because of the British army or navy.
Oh, oh.

That is my opinion, and it is corroborated by the history of past

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
wars in which Canada has been involved. In all probability the answer would be given that preparation for war is an assurance against war. Here again I think the experiences of the last war absolutely demonstrated that such is not the case. If any country was prepared, it was the great country of Germany, and her preparations were absolutely useless, as we all know to-day. Preparation for war is no assurance against war; in fact it is the surest way in which we can be led into war. I think that is the point to which we are coming and to which the thinking of the world is coming. The other day a despatch came from Geneva, and I will read one paragraph of it. Notwithstanding the treaty of Versailles, notwithstanding the Great war, as a matter of fact we are witnessing in Europe greater preparations for war than have existed in almost any other period. This despatch reads:
With the failure of the commission to wring from Europe's leading conscript nations any basis for actual reduction of armies, no greater success was expected with either naval or aerial armaments. That means Europe's five leading nations, England, France, Russia, Italy and Germany, together with Japan, will continue to maintain their present armaments budgets which now average $1,500,000,000 annually, while the world total armaments budget, of which the bulk is European, will remain in the neighborhood of $3,000,000,000 annually.
England alone now is spending nearly $13 per capita annually on armaments; France nearly $6; Italy nearly $4; Japan $3.70; Russia $1.50, and Germany, $1.70. In addition to the direct expenditure, the world's leading conscript nations will continue to deprive their young manhood of one of the most productive periods of its life for military training, while reserve classes up to an advanced age must remain under obligation to sudden summons to the colors.
National Security
The leading conscript nations of the world are France, Italy, Belgium, Poland and CzechoSlovakia. With Japan, those nations, claiming the necessity for national security, have refused to accept any provision that would alter the present size of their armies, decrease their maximum permanent reserves or change their ' conscript systems.

Has my hon. friend compared the figures he has just quoted with the amount of the premiums paid throughout the world for fire protection and fire insurance? Why do we insure our properties against fire? Is it because we want them to be burned?

No, but the parallel is not a good one by any means. Why set fire.,-except as we do sometimes in backfiring on the prairie,-to one comer of your 
building in order to protect the whole building? Why store a powder magazine in one comer of it in order to protect it? By its very nature military preparation is the thing most likely to lead to hostilities. We have recognized that very clearly with regard to quarrels between individuals; we have largely disarmed individuals, and to-day we are safer unarmed than we would be if every man carried a gun.
That is the reason why we have a police force.

Yes, but I would
suggest that as years go on we are resorting less and less to force, and by our social adjustments we are actually removing the need for police of the older type.
If England had not been at least partly prepared for war, if the British ever had the same idea as my hon. friend has enunciated to-day, what would have happened when Germany invaded France?
I do not want to go into that question.
Let me tell my hon. friend that the result would be that Great Britain to-day would be eating sauerkraut.
It is a pretty good dish.

I should have thought that arguments of that kind would not be used during the last two or three years, after so many books have been written dealing with the causes of the last war. A great many people, no doubt, have not yet read the very many interesting and instructive books which have been published in the last few years and which have shown that the stories told during the war were absolutely untrue. I have a long list of those books and if anyone wishes me to quote from them I can do so.
I do not want to enter into that discussion, but I say that England was well prepared; she recognized from the way things were going that war was inevitable, and she took good care to be prepared. But I would say that if she with other nations had sought to remove those causes of friction which everybody knew were present, we would not have had the war at all.

The hon. member says
that England was prepared for war. How many units was she capable of putting into the field?

I have already said I do not intend to go into that.

Private Bills
Tell us.
Let him make his own speech.

England was not so much prepared on land. We know that. British policy for many years was based on the idea that if she were ready with her navy she would be more than a match for any nation that might come against her. She had the greater preparation. I shall be glad to go into that on another occasion.
Seeing the hon. member does not know, probably he would like me to tell him.

There will be an opportunity. Before I close I should like to quote a paragraph which I came across in a little paper sent to me. It is rather pathetic that this should be issued by some unemployed veterans in Canada. I do not know anything about the Veterans' Review, but after speaking of the enormous cost of the war, not only in money but in human life and suffering, the article proceeds:
Altogether it is a tremendous price and should bring a tremendous good to mankind. But no goods have been delivered; the world is not "safe for democracy"; wars are not ended; small nations are in deadly fear; minorities are not protected. On the other hand, there are many Alsace-Lorraines instead of one; wars are everywhere; another great war threatens; and the world is in chaos with suffering, oppression and distrust everywhere. Yet having paid the price, and having been cheated of the thing we bought, we are told we must get ready to pay again a like price to get the same goods.
Those who talk of and prepare for the "next war" are the dangerous men of our time. They should be wholly discredited, however wellmeaning they may be, for their advice and leadership have brought civilization to the verge of the abyss.
Many of the returned men speak in this way. I do not say that the men who have been to the front are the only men who have the right to speak; I think they have the right to speak, for they know at firsthand what war means; but. I would1 say that any man who has made even a superficial study of the horrible evils of war, or who sincerely asks himself what the last war has accomplished, cannot but be anxious to ascertain if there is no other way of settling international disputes.

May I remark that it
saved your liberty?

I do not consider
it saved my liberty one little bit. I would point out that all over the world to-day we are experiencing a period of reaction in almost every department of life. That is due
directly to the war. To-day we are shouldering an enormous burden. As we all know, almost half our national revenue goes to pay for the last war. So I cannot see that that war accomplished anything.
I must thank you, Mr. Chairman, and the committee for your courtesy if I have gone a little far afield. I do not want to impose upon hon. members, but I would say that undoubtedly we cannot settle this cadet vote without having these larger issues in mind. If in the future as in the past war is to be the arbiter of our international disputes, then I say, train every man; let us go even as far as they do in France and train every woman too. I would say further, let us before this session closes pass a law to conscript wealth automatically the moment war is declared. Surely no one can say that wealth is worth more than men.
Yes, they do.

I say it would be
far better before we go any further in training our boys for a future war ho pass a law that the moment war breaks out every dollar in the handls of every man in this country should be conscripted for the service of the state.
Hear, hear.

I think that is the only fair way. I am not here, as some may think, simply to be heard. It is not easy for me to do this. Some of you men can understand, perhaps, how difficult it is for me. But I have boys, as you have boys. It does not make so much difference to some of us; we will not be called to the front, we need not worry about these things; but I want to save my boys. I want them to be brave, I want them to do their duty to their country', but I certainly do not want them t'o become like some of the poor wrecks that survived the last war, and I would not lift my little finger to send my boys into the shambles.
